sections.html:
Concord is New Hampshire's capital and the Merrimack County seat, roughly 16 miles north of Manchester and 66 miles north of Boston. Your tax depends on the city, the county and the school district, so start by finding out which part of Concord the house is in. The villages are Penacook, Concord Heights, East Concord and West Concord, and downtown has a North End and a South End.

Penacook falls in the Merrimack Valley School District instead of the Concord School District. Houses near the Merrimack River and its tributaries should be checked on the FEMA flood map. Winter tests roofs, heating systems and insulation each year, so a seller with an old furnace will hear about it from buyers.

The city bills twice a year but collects in four installments. July and October are estimates, each 25 percent of the prior year's total bill. January and March are final and adjust for the earlier estimates.

InstallmentDue dateType
FirstJuly 1Estimate
SecondOctober 1Estimate
ThirdJanuary 2Final, adjusted
FourthMarch 31Final, adjusted

Expect the July and October bills together around June 1, and the January and March bills around December 1. They rest on the April 1 assessment under RSA 76:2. Late balances accrue 8 percent interest, prorated daily, under state law, and the city has no power to waive it.

Visit the Tax Collector at 41 Green Street or call 603-225-8540. The office opens Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday from 8:00 AM to 4:30 PM, and Thursday from 8:00 AM to 6:00 PM. Payment works online, by phone, in person, or by mail to the City of Concord Tax Office, PO Box 9582, Manchester, NH 03108. Mail it 7 to 10 days early.

Concord charges $29.11 per $1,000 of assessed value for 2025, split as $10.18 for the city, $2.54 for the county, $1.58 for the state education tax and $14.81 for the local school district. The rate was set on November 19, 2025, on a valuation of $4,967,453,081 and a total commitment of $154,257,720.

Your own assessment decides your bill. The local school rate is the largest piece, and if your house is in Penacook or another part of the city, confirm your exact rate with the city assessor at 603-225-8550.

Concord completed a citywide revaluation to bring assessments to full and true market value as of April 1, 2026. The state constitution says values must be set anew at least every five years, and the one before this was in 2021. New assessments are finalized before the final 2026 tax bill in December 2026, and abatement applications are available in the Assessing office after December 1, 2026.

  • Line up your new assessment against recent sales of similar houses.
  • If the number looks wrong, file an abatement application.
  • If you are selling, expect a buyer to underwrite the new value rather than your old one.

Apply to the city for an abatement by March 1 following the notice of tax. Under RSA 76:16, a person aggrieved by an assessment who has complied with RSA 74 may apply in writing by March 1, and the city must grant or deny in writing by July 1. A failure to respond counts as denial. For the current cycle the deadline is March 1, 2027.

If the city denies your request, the denial letter must explain the next appeal step. You can go to the Board of Tax and Land Appeals, phone 603-271-2578, or to superior court. The state sets the abatement form, so get the current one from the city or the Board.

Unpaid tax can turn into a tax lien and eventually a tax deed, though the process takes at least two years. RSA 80:76 has the collector execute a deed to the lienholder two years after the lien if the land has not been redeemed. At least 30 days before that, the collector must notify the owner under RSA 80:77 and mortgage holders under RSA 80:77-a, by certified mail.

A sale that closes while the lien can still be redeemed clears it, since the title company pays the tax from your proceeds. Interest at 8 percent keeps adding to late balances, so a longer wait means a larger payoff.

The state's real estate transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price. Buyer and seller each owe it. Filing and payment happen online through Granite Tax Connect, and the Department of Revenue Administration answers questions at 603-230-5920. Who bears the cost in practice depends on your purchase and sale agreement, so read the closing costs line closely.

Cash is the quickest route to a closing, while a listing can suit a house in good condition. A cash buyer takes the house as-is, which keeps a sale possible when there is deferred roof work, a tenant or a tax balance.

  • Request a payoff statement from your lender and a balance from the Tax Collector.
  • Look up your 2026 assessment and compare it with the old one.
  • Ask for a written offer and see who pays each closing cost.

We buy Concord houses as-is and do not charge commission or fees to the seller.

Concord's tax year is built on the April 1 assessment, and the four installments mean that on any closing date part of the year may already be paid and part may not. Ask the Tax Collector which installments have been paid on your parcel, and ask the title company how it will divide the year between you and the buyer. If your July or October payment was an estimate, remember that the January and March bills adjust for it, so the final figure can differ from what you paid earlier.

Bring the parcel information, the last bill and your lender's payoff statement to the first conversation with the title company. A seller who knows these numbers can read an offer line by line and see what actually lands in the bank.

The Assessing office at 603-225-8550 can tell you whether your 2026 value was set, and whether an abatement application is already on file for the parcel. A buyer's lender will look at the new value, not the old one, so be ready to talk about it.

sections.h2: What buyers will notice in Concord
sections.html:
Concord's villages and neighborhoods shape what buyers expect. A house in Penacook, near Penacook Lake, is a different pitch from one in Concord Heights or the North End. Say which school district applies, mention whether the house is near the Merrimack or the Soucook, and keep your heating and roof records handy. If the 2026 assessment moved your value up or down, expect the buyer to ask about it in the first conversation.

If you own near the Soucook River, the Turkey River or the Contoocook, ask the city whether the flood map affects your parcel and keep the answer on file for the buyer.

faqs.q: When are Concord property taxes due?
faqs.a: The four installments are due July 1, October 1, January 2 and March 31. July and October are estimates at 25 percent of last year's bill, and January and March are final adjusted payments.

faqs.q: What is the Concord tax rate?
faqs.a: The 2025 rate is $29.11 per $1,000: $10.18 city, $2.54 county, $1.58 state education and $14.81 local school.

faqs.q: What is the interest on late Concord property tax?
faqs.a: State law requires 8 percent interest, prorated daily, once a balance passes its due date. The city cannot waive it.

faqs.q: What is the abatement deadline in Concord?
faqs.a: Under RSA 76:16, applications are due by March 1 after the notice of tax. The deadline for the current cycle is March 1, 2027, and forms are available in Assessing after December 1, 2026.

faqs.q: Who pays the New Hampshire transfer tax?
faqs.a: Both of them. Each side pays $0.75 per $100 of the price, filed and paid online through Granite Tax Connect.
